![](Ordinal-Data.jpg)

Here's something I did for years without thinking twice. I'd go into a
field, look at plants, and write down a number from 1 to 5 for how sick
they looked. Then I’d go back to my office, add up all those numbers,
find the average, and say one type of plant was better than another just
because its average was lower.

But the problem is those 1 to 5 numbers were just names I gave to “a
little sick,” “very sick,” and stuff in between. They’re not real
measurements like weight or length. So saying a plant is “2.7 sick”
makes no sense, because no plant can actually be 2.7 sick. That means
averaging them and doing fancy math on them only made it look scientific
when it wasn’t really proving anything.

This guide shows how to:

- Recognize the statistical pitfalls of treating rating scales as
  continuous data
- Understand the mathematical limitations of calculating a mean on
  ordinal categories
- Fit a proportional odds model using the
  [**ordinal**](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ordinal) package in R
- Extract and interpret predicted probabilities for each rating category
- Generate summary visualizations that map the true distribution of your
  data

### Required Packages

We’ll need the following R packages installed and loaded:

```{r setup, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
#| warning: false
library(ordinal)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The problem? Plant scores are "Ordinal Data"

What is ordinal data, really? It's just categories with an order to
them, but no guarantee that the steps between them are equal. Disease
severity 1 to 5, "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree," lodging
scores, a taste panel rating from "hate it" to "love it", all ordinal.
You know 4 is worse than 3, but you have no idea whether the jump from 3
to 4 is the same size as the jump from 1 to 2. It probably isn't.

That's the whole problem with averaging. A mean quietly assumes every
step is worth exactly the same amount, and that the numbers are real
quantities you can add up. Neither is true. The categories only tell you
the order. Anything beyond that is us pretending.

## The fix is easier than you think

Instead of averaging, we fit a model that treats the categories as
categories but still respects their order. The classic one is the
**proportional odds model** (also called a cumulative link model). In R,
it lives in the `ordinal` package, and the function is `clm()`.

The one rule to remember: your response has to be an ordered factor, not
a plain number. That's how you tell R "these have an order, but don't
you dare add them up."

```{r}
#| warning: false

# Fake data to show how it works
plots <- data.frame(
  treatment = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 10),
  severity = c(1,2,2,1,3,2,1,2,3,2,  3,4,3,5,3,4,2,3,4,3) # 1-5 scores
)

# CRITICAL: make severity an ordered factor
plots$severity <- factor(plots$severity, ordered = TRUE)

# Fit the model
model <- clm(severity ~ treatment, data = plots)
summary(model)
```

Here's the part I like. The single treatmentB coefficient of 3.83 is
positive and significant, which just means treatment B pushes plots
toward *higher* severity categories. And those threshold rows (1\|2, 2\|3, ...) are the model
admitting something a mean never could: the cutpoints between categories
aren't evenly spaced. Look at the jumps, the gap from the 2\|3 line to
the 3\|4 line is a bit bigger than from 1\|2 to 2\|3. The model measured
the uneven spacing instead of pretending it away.

## What you get that a mean can't give you

Here's the real payoff. Because the model thinks in categories, you can
ask it for the probability of landing in each severity class — not one
blurry average, but the whole distribution.

```{r}
# Predicted probability of each severity category, per treatment
newdata <- data.frame(treatment = c("A", "B"))
probs <- predict(model, newdata = newdata, type = "prob")$fit
rownames(probs) <- c("A", "B")
round(probs, 3)
```

Read that across. Treatment A spends most of its time in categories 1
and 2 and almost never hits a 5. Treatment B has drained out of the low
end and piled up in 3 and 4. That is so much richer than a single average like "2.7 versus 3.4."
A mean would have quietly hidden the fact that A basically never produces a severe plot at all.

And it plots straight out of the same numbers:

```{r}
plot_df <- data.frame(
  treatment = rep(rownames(probs), times = ncol(probs)),
  severity  = rep(1:5, each = nrow(probs)),
  prob      = as.vector(probs)
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = severity, y = prob, colour = treatment, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.25, position = "identity", linewidth = 0) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_point(size = 3.6, stroke = 1.4, shape = 21, fill = "white") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(A = "#4C9F70", B = "#C1524B"), name = "Treatment") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "#4C9F70", B = "#C1524B"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5,
                     labels = c("1\nhealthy", "2", "3", "4", "5\nsevere")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x * 100, "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .08))) +
  labs(title = "Two treatments, two very different stories",
       subtitle = "Predicted probability of landing in each severity category",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"),
        legend.position = "top", legend.justification = "left")
```

## The one catch you should know about

I'm not going to pretend this model is free. It makes one big
assumption, and it's worth a paragraph: the proportional odds
assumption. In plain terms, it assumes a treatment shoves every category
boundary in the same direction by the same amount. It can't decide to
bump you from mild to moderate but not from moderate to severe — it
moves the whole scale together.

Sometimes that's not realistic, so it's worth a quick check. Fair warning
though, this test needs more data than our toy example has. With 20 plots
spread across 5 categories it just returns blanks. So let's borrow the
`wine` dataset that ships with the package:

```{r}
data(wine)   # comes with the package

model_wine <- clm(rating ~ temp + contact, data = wine)

# Does the proportional odds assumption hold?
nominal_test(model_wine)
```

The p-values for `temp` and `contact` are what you care about here. Both
are comfortably above 0.05, which means there's no evidence the assumption
is broken, so you're fine. If one of them came back small (say under 0.05), that variable is
misbehaving, and you'd let it off the leash with a *partial*
proportional odds model (the `nominal =` argument in `clm()`). But
honestly? Nine times out of ten in field data, the basic model is
plenty. Don't let the assumption scare you off — just check it, note it,
and move on.

## But my t-test gave me a p-value too

Fair. Let's actually run the wrong way and the right way side by side on
the same data and see what happens.

```{r}
data(wine)

# THE WRONG WAY: pretend the rating is a number, run a t-test
wine$rating_num <- as.numeric(as.character(wine$rating))
t.test(rating_num ~ temp, data = wine)

# THE RIGHT WAY: ordinal model
model_temp <- clm(rating ~ temp, data = wine)
summary(model_temp)
```

The t-test tells you cold wine averaged 2.33 and warm averaged 3.50, p =
0.0000007. The ordinal model also says warm wine rates significantly
higher (p \< 0.0001). So did the t-test "work"?

Sort of. And this is the honest part I want to leave you with: the mean
isn't evil. When the effect is big and the categories are roughly evenly
spaced, a t-test will often point the same direction. It's not that
you'll always get the wrong answer — it's that you get a thinner one.
"2.33 versus 3.50" quietly invents a precision the data never had, and
it can't tell you that warm wine almost never gets a bottom rating while
cold wine almost never gets a top one. Same data, but the ordinal model
actually respects what the numbers are.

## The takeaway

Here's the reframe I wish someone had handed me years ago: your rating
scale was never a ruler. Those 1 to 5 disease scores, the "disagree to
agree" survey columns, the lodging ratings — they're ranks in a costume,
ordered labels doing their best impression of real numbers. A mean takes
that costume at face value. An ordinal model doesn't.

The nice surprise is that respecting your data doesn't cost you
anything. It's one package, one `factor(..., ordered = TRUE)`, and one
function. In exchange you stop reporting averages nobody can picture,
and you start reporting something a person can actually see: how likely
each treatment is to land in each category.

So next time you're about to take the mean of a rating scale — don't.
Fit the model that knows those numbers are only pretending. Your data
will thank you, and so will whoever reviews your paper.

## Want to go deeper?

If any of this made you want to actually learn the machinery rather than
just copy my code, here's where I'd send you, roughly in order of how
gently they ease you in:

- [**Cumulative Link Models for Ordinal Regression with the R Package
  ordinal**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ordinal/vignettes/clm_article.pdf)
  — Rune Christensen wrote the package, and this is his own walkthrough
  of it. It uses that same wine bitterness dataset from Randall (1989) —
  a factorial experiment where nine judges rated wine from four
  treatment conditions, 72 observations in all. Start here.

- [**Summary and Analysis of Extension Program Evaluation in R
  (Mangiafico)**](https://rcompanion.org/handbook/G_01.html) — the
  friendliest intro I know, and it's aimed squarely at ag and extension
  folks. It also covers the proportional odds assumption and the
  `nominal_test` and `scale_test` functions we used above.

- [**McCullagh (1980), *Regression Models for Ordinal
  Data***](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2984952) — the original paper.
  Dense, but it's where the proportional odds model comes from, and it's
  worth knowing the source.

- [**The `ordinal` package
  itself**](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=ordinal) — the reference
  manual, plus the mixed-model side of things if your ratings are nested
  (multiple judges, repeated plots, split-plot designs). That's
  `clmm()`, and it's the natural next step once you outgrow `clm()`.
